title: Retail Payment Operations in Southeast Asia: A Guide for Global Retailers Scaling Across Markets
summary: Retail payments in Southeast Asia get complex across stores and markets. Learn what your payment operation needs before you scale.
body_markdown:
Retail payments in Southeast Asia become harder to manage the moment your business


**operates across several markets** at once. A


**global retailer** entering the region may sell through e-commerce, run physical stores, carry more than one brand, and operate through franchise or subsidiary structures at the same time.


Payment activity then does not happen in one place. Your retail business may need to


**collect payments across channels** ,


**process refunds and returns after the sale** ,


**settle funds to different entities** , and


**reconcile transactions across markets** . Each of those flows carries its own records, timelines, and local requirements.


As the retail operation grows, handling them separately by country, channel, or entity turns into


**fragmented work** for finance and operations, and the fragmentation grows with every store, brand, and market added.


The volume moving through those channels keeps growing at the same time.


[Southeast Asia's digital economy](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/e_conomy_sea_2025_report.pdf) is on track to surpass


**USD 300 billion in gross merchandise value** , around 1.5 times the inaugural forecast made ten years ago, with both GMV and revenue growing about


**15% year over year** . For your business, that growth arrives as transaction volume spreads across more channels and more markets, which moves


**payment management** into an operational concern that extends well past the checkout page.


Choosing which payment methods to activate in each country is only one part of the decision. The bigger question is whether your payment operation can support the way a retail business runs across the region, with multiple channels, entities, refund paths, and demand peaks happening at the same time.


**Here is what this article covers:**


- Where retail payment operations fragment across channels, returns, entities, and peak periods in Southeast Asia


- The capabilities to check before your payment setup has to carry a regional retail operation


- A short framework to work through before entering or scaling a market


- How Xendit supports acceptance, visibility, refunds, and fund routing across our operating markets


- How to keep the customer-facing payment experience local while the operation behind it stays consistent


## **What makes retail payment operations difficult across Southeast Asia**


Retail payment complexity is easier to manage once you understand where it comes from.


**Four conditions turn a working payment setup into a fragmented one** for retailers operating across Southeast Asia:


### **Payments come from more sales channels than the setup was built for**


Retailers increasingly sell online and offline at the same time, and one customer journey can involve several payment touchpoints, including a brand website, a marketplace listing, a store counter, or a checkout inside a live video session.


**Live and video shopping** has become a sales channel of its own, and it now accounts for


[25%](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/e_conomy_sea_2025_report.pdf) of total e-commerce GMV in the region. For your business, the online side of retail can already mean a website, a marketplace listing, and a livestream checkout, and each of them produces its own payment records, refund paths, and settlement lines that have to stay connected to the rest.


**In-store payments** have changed in the same period. Ten Southeast Asian countries now run


[national QR systems](https://services.google.com/fh/files/misc/e_conomy_sea_2025_report.pdf) with strong adoption, and eight markets support cross-border QR interoperability. For a retailer with physical stores, QR acceptance at the counter has become a standard requirement in each market, and a store in one country can now take payment from a customer using an app registered in another, which adds another transaction type for your finance team to recognize in reporting.


Keeping payment records, refunds, and settlement information connected across channels then becomes an operational requirement for your business, so every transaction can be traced back to the purchase behind it.


### **Returns and refunds sometimes happen through a different channel from the purchase**


A retail transaction does not end when the payment completes. Returns, cancellations, exchanges, and partial refunds may happen


**days or weeks after the purchase** , and often


**through a different channel** , such as an item bought on the website and brought back to a store. Finance teams then have to connect the purchase record with the refund that follows it, and that connection is harder to maintain across multiple markets and payment methods.


Refund support and refund windows differ by channel. With Xendit, for example,


[card refunds](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) run to 365 days across markets, GCash in the Philippines allows 180 days, QRIS in Indonesia allows 30 days, and several bank transfer, virtual account, and over-the-counter channels do not support refunds at all. For your business, a returns policy written without checking those differences creates store-level exceptions that finance resolves manually later.


### **One retail group can hold several brands and entities**


Global retailers often operate multiple brands, subsidiaries, franchise locations, or legal entities under one group. Payments collected under each of them may need to be routed, held, and accounted for separately, even when the checkout looks identical to the customer.


Accepting the payment is one problem, but directing the funds to the correct entity with a record your accountants can follow is a second one, and it becomes visible when routing depends on manual transfers after settlement. Every new store, brand, or franchise partner then adds work to a process that was already manual.


***Also read:[The Multi-Entity Reconciliation Guide for Businesses Operating Across Southeast Asia](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/the-multi-entity-reconciliation-guide-for-businesses-operating-across-southeast-asia/)***


### **Fragmented payment operations cost more during high-demand periods**


Retail sales concentrate around a few dates each quarter, including campaign days, seasonal sales, product launches, and holiday trading. Those dates can carry a large share of quarterly revenue, with refund volume rising in the weeks after.


A payment operation that performs at normal volume still has to work through those days. Payment failures and limited visibility cost more when revenue is concentrated, because the response has to happen while the campaign is still running and the same teams are already handling higher store and service volume.


***Also read:[Enterprise Payment Infrastructure for Peak E-Commerce Traffic: A Southeast Asia Guide](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/enterprise-payment-infrastructure-for-peak-e-commerce-traffic-a-southeast-asia-guide/)***


Multiple sales channels, refunds that arrive later, multi-entity structures, and concentrated demand all point to the same requirement. Before comparing providers on payment method coverage, define what your payment operation needs to do.


## **What your retail payment operation should be able to handle**


The more useful evaluation question changes the subject from coverage to fit. Instead of asking which payment methods you need in each market, ask whether the payment operation can support the way your retail business already works.


**Five payment capabilities** decide whether that operation can carry a retail business across Southeast Asia:


- **Cross-channel payment visibility** **** **** Your finance team needs to see payment activity from


**online** **and** **physical retail channels** in one place, and to follow a single transaction through


**payment** ,


**settlement** ,


**refund** , and


**reconciliation** . When that view is split across a different system for every channel, the link between a sale and its settlement record has to be rebuilt manually at month-end. The test is whether your team can say where a specific transaction stands without opening more than one dashboard.


- **Flexible fund routing** Payments should reach the right


**brand** ,


**entity** ,


**franchise** , or


**business unit** as part of the transaction itself. Retail groups rarely use one ownership structure across a region, so the setup also has to handle stores that are company-owned, franchised, or run by a local partner.


**Routing** that depends on manual transfers after settlement adds finance work with every location you open.


- **Connected refunds and returns** Refunds need to stay


**linked to the purchase** they came from, using the same reference the sale carried. That link is what lets your team reconcile returns


**across channels and payment methods** without matching amounts manually. It carries more work in retail than in most industries, because return rates are predictable and the volume is continuous.


- **Regional operational consistency** One operating model across the region


**keeps reporting, refund handling, and reconciliation the same in every market** , while the payment methods on the customer's screen stay local. Without it, each country develops its own process, and consolidation becomes a separate exercise every month. The test here is whether your business can add a market without also adding a new way of working.


- **Reliability at retail scale** **Payment processing** has to absorb sharp increases in transaction activity


**without disruption** , since retail volume concentrates around campaigns and peak trading hours. Your team also needs enough


**visibility** to find and fix a payment issue while the revenue is still recoverable, which means transaction status and failure reasons available while the campaign is still running. V


isibility, fund routing, refund handling, regional consistency, and reliability together show where a retail payment setup will strain first.

## **A practical framework before entering or scaling a Southeast Asian market**


Those requirements discussed above look different once they are applied to a specific country, because each market in the region brings its own payment habits, store footprint, and entity setup.


Before your business opens payments in a new market or adds another brand to an existing one,


**five questions** surface most of the operational work early:


- **Customer payment journey** Where and how will customers pay in this market, online, in store, or across both, and which local methods carry the volume?


- **Payment operations** How will transactions, refunds, settlements, and reconciliation be managed across those channels?


- **Entity and brand structure** Where should funds go when the business runs multiple brands, entities, or franchise locations?


- **Regional scalabilityC** an the same operating model support the next market without creating a disconnected process?
- **Peak-period readiness** Can the operation hold reliability and visibility when transaction volume rises sharply?


Working through these questions before you launch in a new Southeast Asian market lets your team build the payment setup around the answers. Leaving them until after launch usually means finance is the one covering the gaps at month-end.


## **How Xendit supports retail payment operations across Southeast Asia**


Xendit supports businesses operating in Indonesia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand, Malaysia, and Singapore, with coverage extending beyond Southeast Asia as well. Xendit also offer capabilities to address the retail payment challenges covered above:


### **1. Payment acceptance for in-store and online channels**


Xendit gives your business access to


[more than 100 payment methods](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) through


**one integration** , covering what customers in each market use, such as virtual accounts, QRIS, and e-wallets such as OVO, DANA, and ShopeePay in Indonesia, GCash, Maya, online banking, and over-the-counter payments in the Philippines, PromptPay in Thailand, FPX in Malaysia, PayNow in Singapore, MoMo and ZaloPay in Vietnam, and cards across markets.


Physical stores carry one requirement that online checkout does not. A counter needs a payment code that can be used more than once, and several


[payment channels available through Xendit](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) support a reusable payment code, so one code can collect multiple payments, for example a static QR displayed at a till.


How your business connects to Xendit depends on how your commerce stack is built.


[Payment links](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/payment-links/) cover payment collection without engineering work,


[plug-ins](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-plug-ins-work) cover platform-native operators running Shopify, WooCommerce, Magento, or Wix, and


[payment API](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/how-payments-api-work) covers brand.com operators on a proprietary stack. Your business can vary the customer-facing payment mix by market and by channel while the integration behind it stays the same.


### **2. Transaction visibility and account structure for finance teams**


[XenPlatform](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/xenplatform/) lets your business create account hierarchies, with


[sub-accounts](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/sub-accounts) representing stores, brands, subsidiaries, or business units, each holding its own balance and transaction history. The head office keeps a


**consolidated view** through


**centralized reporting** and can decide how much dashboard access each account holds.


[Mekari](https://www.xendit.co/en/case-study/mekari/) , which runs payments for thousands of merchants, reduced the manpower needed for reconciliation by 60% and made monthly reconciliation five times faster after moving to this structure.


For a retail group, that separation is what lets finance report by store or by brand without asking every location to send its own file.

### **3. Refunds that stay attached to the original transaction**


Xendit's


[refund API](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/refund-payment-request) creates the refund against the payment request ID of the original payment, so the adjustment carries the reference of the transaction it belongs to. Refunds return to the original payment method, and funds cannot be sent to a different card or bank account, which keeps the return path predictable for finance and customer service.


Two things need to be built into your returns process:


- **Check the refund window per channel** Refund validity differs across payment channels, so the channel directory should be checked against the returns window you publish in each market.


- **Separate the refund status from the money landing** Once a refund is submitted, Xendit sends your systems a[webhook notification](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/refund-payment-request) , an automated status message confirming whether Xendit processed the request and passed it to the payment channel. When the funds reach the customer's account depends on the issuer or channel partner, so your store staff can set customer expectations on that basis instead of promising a timeline the channel controls.


### **4. Fund routing for multi-brand and franchise structures**


[Split Payments](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) lets your business


**route incoming funds** according to how the group is actually structured. You create a split rule with a flat or percentage amount, set the destination account, and apply the rule at transaction level, with several routes possible inside a single transaction.


A retail group running franchise stores can run two rules side by side, taking a flat fee per transaction from stores in one city and a percentage of revenue from stores in another.


**Each route reports its own status** through a webhook, and both split rules and processed splits can be tracked and exported from the dashboard.


Refunds need a decision here as well as split fees are not returned automatically when the original payment is refunded, so agree with each brand or franchise partner how those fees are handled on refunds and chargebacks before volume builds.


### **5. Processing reliability when retail volume concentrates**


Xendit reports


[99.999% payment uptime](https://www.xendit.co/en/blog/xendit-payment-reliability-99-999-uptime/) , maintained by a dedicated engineering team. For a retailer, that


**reliability** matters most on campaign days and during peak store trading hours, when a failed payment costs a sale already standing at the counter and creates follow-up work for teams handling higher volume.


### **6. Licensed entities in each operating market**


Xendit holds


[licenses through local entities](https://www.xendit.co/en-id/company/xendit-licenses-2/) across our operating markets, with the full list published by country. For global retailers,


**licensing affects two things** :


- **Vendor review** The documentation your legal, risk, and procurement teams check before payment acceptance goes live.


- **Market entry** Allowing local collection and settlement to run under each country's rules, so opening a new market does not start with finding a separate licensed provider.


Capability describes what the infrastructure can do. Applying it market by market takes a shorter set of questions.

## **FAQ for global retailers in Southeast Asia: Retail payment operations**


### **How can a retailer accept in-store payments across Southeast Asia without a separate setup in each market?**


Local payment habits differ by country, so in-store acceptance depends on offering what customers already carry.


**Xendit** gives your business access to


[local payment channels](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/all-payment-methods/) across our operating markets through one integration, and several of


[those channels](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) support a reusable payment code, so a single code can collect multiple payments at a counter. The method mix at store level can change by country while the connection behind it stays the same.


### **Can a customer return an online purchase in a physical store and still be refunded?**


Yes, and the refund still returns to the method the customer originally paid with, even when the return happens through a different channel from the sale.


**Xendit** creates


[refunds](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/refund-payment-request) against the original payment request ID, and channels that support it also allow partial and multiple partial refunds for part-order returns. Your store and service teams need the original payment reference on hand, so it belongs in the order record your point of sale can look up.


### **How can a retail group send payments to the right brand, franchise, or store entity?**


Routing works best when it happens as part of the transaction.


**Xendit's**[split payments](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/split-payments) let your business create flat or percentage split rules, set a destination account for each route, and apply several routes to one transaction, which covers franchise fees, brand-level revenue, and platform commissions. Each route sends its own status webhook and can be exported from the Split Payments dashboard for reconciliation.


### **How long does it take for retail payments to settle in Southeast Asia?**


[Settlement time](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/available-payment-channels) depends on the payment channel. Some channels settle instantly, including several virtual accounts in Indonesia and PromptPay in Thailand, QR and e-wallet channels commonly settle on T plus 2 business days, and cards settle on T plus 5 business days, so one day of store trading can settle across several dates.


**Xendit** also offers early settlement, which releases funds ahead of the standard window and helps retail teams manage working capital across locations


### **Can a global retailer keep funds in each market or settle them to a central HQ entity?**


Both are supported, and the right choice usually depends on where the business holds local obligations such as supplier payments, rent, and payroll.


**Xendit** offers


[flexible settlement arrangements](https://docs.xendit.co/docs/settlements-overview) , including settlement in country or to a central entity, and


[Xendit Cross Border](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/cross-border-payments/) lets your business collect in local currencies and send cross-border payouts through one API. Availability depends on eligibility and the regulatory requirements in each country, so confirm the setup market by market with our team.


### **How do finance teams reconcile store, marketplace, and website transactions in one place?**


Reconciliation gets easier when each transaction already carries its channel, fee, settlement status, and your own reference in one record. With


[XenPlatform](https://www.xendit.co/en/products/xenplatform/) , your business can hold sub-accounts for stores, brands, or subsidiaries, each with its own balance and transaction history, while head office exports consolidated reports across accounts. Your finance team then reviews the exceptions instead of assembling a separate report for every channel.
